modal_intro.title: The Astronomical Clock 🧭
modal_intro.headline: The Astronomical Clock of St. Mary's in Lübeck: Simulation
modal_intro.welcome: Welcome to the interactive simulation of the Astronomical Clock of St. Mary's Church in Lübeck. This model invites you to explore the clock's functions yourself.
modal_intro.overview_text: The astronomical clock in Lübeck's St. Mary's Church, completed in 1976, serves multiple purposes and displays a wealth of astronomical and calendrical data.
modal_intro.dial_text: The central clock dial displays astronomical conditions with great precision.
modal_intro.dial_time: The sun pointer shows the time on a 2×I...XII numeral ring and completes one revolution in 24 hours.
modal_intro.dial_sun_moon: The actual astronomical positions of the sun and moon in the starry sky are displayed.
modal_intro.dial_zodiac: Shows the 13 constellations of the zodiac in their natural extent.
modal_intro.dial_moonphase: The current phase is shown by a half-bright, half-dark sphere on the moon pointer.
modal_intro.calendar_text: The lower part is the calendar. The calendar disc contains the 13 zodiac constellations on the outside.
modal_intro.calendar_rings: Day letters, month names, day dates, ecclesiastical day names.
modal_intro.calendar_year: Year ring (1911 to 2080), Sunday letters, Golden Numbers, Easter dates.
modal_intro.calendar_leap: The clockwork accounts for February 29th in leap years.
modal_intro.calendar_eclipse: Solar and lunar eclipses for the period 2000 to 2036 are shown.
modal_intro.figure_text: The superstructure contains the procession of figures and iconographic representations.
modal_intro.figure_procession: At noon, eight figures representing people from different parts of the world pass in front of the central Christ figure.
modal_intro.figure_bell: The hour bell is struck by a figure of an old man with an hourglass.
modal_intro.figure_icons: The figures represent symbols of time, transience, and Christian virtues.
modal_intro.controls_text: You can control the simulation and retrieve important calendar information.
modal_intro.ctrl_sim_date: Enter a specific date and time.
modal_intro.ctrl_sim_now: Immediately resets the clock to the current system time.
modal_intro.ctrl_cal_data: Displays the calculated calendar data for the currently set date.
modal_intro.ctrl_cal_eclipse: Lists the solar and lunar eclipses for the currently set year.
modal_intro.ctrl_btn_cal: Explains how the historical clock calculates the day of the week.
modal_intro.ctrl_btn_hist: Provides background information on the history and restoration of the clock.
modal_intro.tech_data: Calendar data and eclipses are limited to the period 1911 to 2080.
modal_intro.tech_browser: The simulation was developed for modern browsers and uses the Canvas API.
modal_intro.tech_mobile: On smaller screens, the controls are collapsed by default.
modal_intro.symbols_intro: To save space, the compact calendar overview uses symbols instead of spelled-out terms (details appear as a tooltip on tap/hover):

modal_calendar.title: The Calendar Disc
modal_calendar.intro: The calendar disc is divided into several circles. In the outer circle, alongside the 366 days of the year, large red letters appear: ABCDEFG. These seven letters indicate the days of the week.
modal_calendar.inner: The innermost ring shows the dates of Easter Sundays. Between them are the so-called Golden Numbers, indicating the year's position in the 19-year lunar cycle.
modal_calendar.rule_intro: A Sunday letter (SL) means that all days marked with that letter are Sundays. Monday is the next letter, Tuesday the one after, and so on.
modal_calendar.step2_title: Step 2: Count from SL to DL ⏱️
modal_calendar.step2_text: Start counting at the valid Sunday letter and count forward until the day letter is reached.
modal_calendar.step3_text: The day of the week results from the position in the count (position 0 = Sunday, position 6 = Saturday).
modal_calendar.golden_number_info: After 19 years, the phases of the moon repeat on nearly the same calendar days. The Golden Number plays an important role in calculating the date of Easter and other movable church holidays. Together with other calendrical rules, it helps determine the first full moon after the beginning of spring, on the Sunday following which Easter is celebrated.

modal_history.title: Art & History of the Astronomical Clock 📜
modal_history.headline: The History of the Astronomical Clock 📜
modal_history.intro: The clock in St. Mary's stands in a long tradition of representation and innovation in the Hanseatic city of Lübeck.
modal_history.clock1_text: The first astronomical clock, consisting of a calendar disc and planetarium, was put into operation. A surviving relic, the carved zodiac, is displayed today in the St. Anne's Museum.
modal_history.clock2_text: Matthias van Oß built the second, even more representative clock, distinguished by rich carvings by Hinrich Matthes and the famous Electors' Procession.
modal_history.clock3_text: The tower clock factory Eduard Korfhage renewed the mechanism in 1889–1890. Due to the old clockwork, the calendar disc had to be manually reset on March 1st every leap year.
modal_history.clock4_text: The historical clock was completely destroyed on Palm Sunday (March 29th) 1942 during the bombing of Lübeck.
modal_history.img_title: 📷 The preserved clockwork in the St. Anne's Museum, Lübeck
modal_history.img_subtitle: Remains of the first astronomical clock from 1405 — zodiac disc with gilded figures, gears and hands. The lower wheel is the drive wheel of the clockwork.
modal_history.rebuild1_text: The new construction was primarily initiated and planned by Paul Behrens, who closely modelled the exterior on the historical original.
modal_history.rebuild2_text: Behrens purchased a well-preserved older tower clock mechanism and restored it. The pointer mechanism and the figure procession systems were newly manufactured.
modal_history.rebuild3_text: The new clock was set in motion in 1967 and finally completed in 1976. The data on the central disc ranges from 1911 to 2080.
modal_history.art_intro: The clock follows the characteristic three-part division of medieval astronomical clocks: calendar at the bottom, clock dial in the middle, and figure procession at the top.
modal_history.art_center_text: The centre of the planetarium features the figure of the Saviour (Christ) emerging from clouds and rays, alluding to the Gospel of John.
modal_history.art_zodiac_text: The copper-embossed sun and moon move astronomically correctly through the zodiac. The ring encompasses 13 constellations, including Ophiuchus (the Serpent Bearer).
modal_history.art_craft_text: The figures were made by master carpenter Heinrich Brand; the gilding was applied by master painter Alfred Mundt.
modal_history.inscription_text: AS OFTEN AS YOU HEAR THE RINGING BELL, DO NOT FORGET YOUR GOD WHO RULES OVER ALL THE STARS, TO PRAISE AND THANK HIM
modal_history.fig1_text: Instead of the Electors of the predecessor model, the figures now show the 'Believers of the World' — created by Marianne Schmidt.
modal_history.fig2_text: They emerge from the left door, bow before Christ and are blessed by him.
modal_history.fig3_text: Carved by Fritz Block. The hour bell is struck by an old man with an hourglass. The Janus figure (old man / young woman) alludes to the past and the future.
modal_history.img_giebel_title: 📷 The Figure Superstructure and Gable of the Astronomical Clock
modal_history.img_giebel_subtitle: The crowning gable with the figure procession, as it appears today in St. Mary's Church.
modal_history.img_getriebe_title: 📷 The Gearing of the Astronomical Clock
modal_history.img_getriebe_subtitle: View of the gear train that drives the pointer mechanism and figure procession in sync.
modal_history.img_uhrwerk_subtitle: The tower clock mechanism, restored by Paul Behrens, running since 1967.

luebeck_rule.uses_letters: The year {year} uses the letters {a} (Jan/Feb) and {b} (from March).
luebeck_rule.because_before: Since {day}. {month} is before March 1st, the letter {sb} applies.
luebeck_rule.because_after: Since {day}. {month} is after February 28th, the letter {sb} applies.
luebeck_rule.uniform: For the year {year} a uniform Sunday letter applies: {sb}.
